Senses.Explanation: In the inherited guest-dust image, ‘guest’ and ‘dust’ name transient troubles or stain that arrive and depart rather than the host. Literally, “guest-dust”: dust characterized as a visitor rather than the host. Much of the corpus preserves it in the inherited compound “guest-dust troubles” (客塵煩惱), something said to stain, cover, or be unrecognized. Baizhang Huaihai's distinct functional classification is separated into the Baizhang-specific sense below. Elsewhere the Records say a grown child learns explanations and does not know that these are “guest-dust troubles” (不知是客塵煩惱); Dahui speaks of the “stain of guest-dust troubles since beginningless time” (無始時來客塵煩惱之染); and the Admonitions for the Monastic Gate has the compact bodily compound “body-and-mind guest-dust” (身心客塵). The Zen record therefore keeps the inherited dust imagery while Baizhang bends the compound into an explicit ruler/function classification.
Senses.Note: The corpus-wide sense remains one article because the Baizhang classification depends on the same guest-versus-ruler morphology as the broader compound. The explanation describes the recorded classification without adding an outside account of affliction or purity.

Senses.Explanation: To inspect is to check a saying, action, person, or one's own handling closely enough to call faults and adequacy into account. Teachers use the word when reviewing old cases, rebuking an interlocutor, or warning the assembly to examine what has just been said.
